title: 2  Hilbert space for random vectors
text:
2.2 Chapter Summary
This chapter introduces the Hilbert space of \(q\)-dimensional random functions \(h(Z)\) with mean zero and finite second moments:
\[
E\{h(Z)\} = 0,
\qquad
E\{h^\top(Z)h(Z)\} < \infty.
\]
The covariance inner product is defined by
\[
\langle h_1, h_2\rangle
=
E(h_1^\top h_2),
\]
with corresponding norm
\[
\|h\|
=
\langle h,h\rangle^{1/2}.
\]
Two elements are orthogonal when their inner product is zero. For a closed linear subspace \(\mathcal{U}\subset\mathcal{H}\), the projection theorem guarantees a unique projection \(\Pi(h\mid\mathcal{U})\in\mathcal{U}\) such that
\[
\Pi(h\mid\mathcal{U})
=
\arg\min_{u\in\mathcal{U}}
\|h-u\|.
\]
The residual after projection is orthogonal to the subspace:
\[
h-\Pi(h\mid\mathcal{U})
\perp
\mathcal{U}.
\]
For a finite-dimensional subspace spanned by a random vector \(u(Z)\), the projection is a linear function of \(u\), whose coefficients are determined by the variance of \(u(Z)\) and its covariance with \(h(Z)\) (see (2.1) below).

title: 2  Hilbert space for random vectors
text:
2.3 Notes and Extensions

2.3.1 Projection onto linear span vs conditional expectation
By definition,
\[
\Pi\{h(Z)\mid\mathcal{U}\}
=
\arg\min_{g\in\mathcal{U}}\|h-g\|,
\]
for any closed linear subspace \(\mathcal{U}\subset\mathcal{H}\). That is, the projection of \(h(Z)\) onto \(\mathcal{U}\) is the element of \(\mathcal{U}\) closest to \(h(Z)\) in the norm \(\|\cdot\|\).
Example 1 in Tsiatis (2006) considers the linear span
\[
\mathcal{U}
=
\left\{
a^{\top}u
:
a\in\mathbb{R}^k
\right\}
\]
of a \(k\)-dimensional random vector
\[
u(Z)
=
\{u_1(Z),\ldots,u_k(Z)\}^{\top}.
\]
It establishes that
\[
\Pi\{h(Z)\mid\mathcal{U}\}
=
E(hu^{\top})
\left\{
E(uu^{\top})
\right\}^{-1}
u.
\tag{2.1}\]
If \(\mathcal{U}\) is expanded to include all measurable square-integrable functions of \(u(Z)\), the projection is the conditional expectation of \(h(Z)\) given \(u(Z)\) (Tsiatis, 2006). Specifically,
\[
E\{h(Z)\mid u\}
=
\Pi\{h(Z)\mid\mathcal{U}^*\}
=
\arg\min_{g\in\mathcal{U}^*}
\|h-g\|,
\]
where
\[
\mathcal{U}^*
=
\left\{
a(u)
:
a(\cdot) \text{ is a measurable and square-integrable function on }
\mathbb{R}^k
\right\}.
\]
Because \(\mathcal{U}\subset\mathcal{U}^*\), the best approximation of \(h(Z)\) in \(\mathcal{U}^*\) is at least as good as the best approximation in \(\mathcal{U}\). Thus,
\[
\left\|
h-E\{h(Z)\mid u\}
\right\|
\leq
\left\|
h-\Pi\{h(Z)\mid\mathcal{U}\}
\right\|.
\]
By a standard property of the multivariate normal distribution, \(E\{h(Z)\mid u\}\) is linear in \(u\) when \(h(Z)\) and \(u(Z)\) are jointly multivariate normal. In this case,
\[
E\{h(Z)\mid u\}
=
\Pi\{h(Z)\mid\mathcal{U}\},
\] which is in turn given by (2.1).


2.3.2 Dimensionality of \(\mathcal{U}=\{Bv:B\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times r}\}\)
Here, \(v\) is an \(r\)-dimensional random vector. On page 17, it is claimed that \(\mathcal{U}\) is \(q\times r\)-dimensional because it is the linear span of that many linearly independent functions.
Indeed, a typical element of \(\mathcal{U}\) is given by \[
\begin{aligned}
u
= Bv =
\begin{pmatrix}
\sum_{j=1}^r B_{1j}v_j \\
\sum_{j=1}^r B_{2j}v_j \\
\vdots \\
\sum_{j=1}^r B_{qj}v_j
\end{pmatrix}
=
\sum_{j=1}^r
\begin{pmatrix}
B_{1j}v_j \\
B_{2j}v_j \\
\vdots \\
B_{qj}v_j
\end{pmatrix}
=
\sum_{j=1}^r\sum_{i=1}^q
B_{ij} u_{ij}^{q\times 1},
\end{aligned}
\]
where \[
u_{ij}^{q\times 1} = (\underbrace{0,\ldots, 0}_{i-1}， v_j, \underbrace{0， \ldots, 0}_{q-i})^\top,
\] as defined in the book.

title: 2  Hilbert space for random vectors
text:
2.4 Solutions to Exercises

2.4.1 Exercise 2.1

Solution. Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a closed linear subspace of the Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\), and let \(h\in\mathcal{H}\). We prove:

Existence: There exists \(u_0\in\mathcal{U}\) such that
\[
\|h-u_0\|
=
\inf_{u\in\mathcal{U}}
\|h-u\|.
\]
Uniqueness: The minimizer \(u_0\) is unique.
Orthogonality: The residual is orthogonal to \(\mathcal{U}\):
\[
\langle h-u_0,u\rangle = 0
\qquad
\text{for every } u\in\mathcal{U}.
\]

To show existence, let
\[
d
=
\inf_{u\in\mathcal{U}}
\|h-u\|.
\]
Choose a sequence \(\{u_n\}\subset\mathcal{U}\) such that
\[
\|h-u_n\| \longrightarrow d.
\]
We first show that \(\{u_n\}\) is a Cauchy sequence. Because \((u_n+u_m)/2\in\mathcal{U}\),
\[
d
\leq
\left\|
h-\frac{u_n+u_m}{2}
\right\|.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|u_n-u_m\|^2
&=
\left\|
(h-u_n)-(h-u_m)
\right\|^2 \\
&=
\|h-u_n\|^2
+
\|h-u_m\|^2
-
2\langle h-u_n,h-u_m\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
4d^2
&\leq
4\left\|
h-\frac{u_n+u_m}{2}
\right\|^2 \\
&=
\left\|
(h-u_n)+(h-u_m)
\right\|^2 \\
&=
\|h-u_n\|^2
+
\|h-u_m\|^2
+
2\langle h-u_n,h-u_m\rangle \\
&=
2\|h-u_n\|^2
+
2\|h-u_m\|^2
-
\|u_n-u_m\|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|u_n-u_m\|^2
&\leq
2\|h-u_n\|^2
+
2\|h-u_m\|^2
-
4d^2 \\
&\longrightarrow 0
\qquad
\text{as } n,m\longrightarrow\infty.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, \(\{u_n\}\) is Cauchy. Since \(\mathcal{H}\) is complete, there exists \(u_0\in\mathcal{H}\) such that
\[
u_n\longrightarrow u_0.
\]
Because \(\mathcal{U}\) is closed and \(u_n\in\mathcal{U}\) for every \(n\),
\[
u_0\in\mathcal{U}.
\]
By continuity of the norm,
\[
\|h-u_0\|
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}\|h-u_n\|
=
d.
\]
This establishes existence.
To show orthogonality, fix \(u\in\mathcal{U}\) and define
\[
g(\epsilon)
=
\|h-(u_0-\epsilon u)\|^2.
\]
Since \(u_0-\epsilon u\in\mathcal{U}\) for every \(\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}\), \(g(\epsilon)\) is minimized at \(\epsilon=0\). Hence,
\[
\begin{aligned}
0
&=
\left.
\frac{\partial}{\partial\epsilon}
g(\epsilon)
\right|_{\epsilon=0} \\
&=
2\langle h-u_0,u\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore,
\[
\langle h-u_0,u\rangle=0
\qquad
\text{for every } u\in\mathcal{U}.
\]
Finally, for uniqueness, suppose that \(u_0\) and \(u_0^*\) both minimize \(\|h-u\|\) over \(\mathcal{U}\). Since \(u_0-u_0^*\in\mathcal{U}\), orthogonality gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|h-u_0^*\|^2
&=
\underbrace{\|h-u_0\|^2}_{d^2}
+
\underbrace{\|u_0-u_0^*\|^2}_{\geq 0}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(\|h-u_0^*\|^2=d^2\), it follows that
\[
\|u_0-u_0^*\|^2=0,
\]
and hence \(u_0=u_0^*\).



2.4.2 Exercise 2.2

Solution. This exercise is a direct application of Example 2 in the book.

Because \(\Sigma_{22}=E(Y_2Y_2^{\mathsf T})\) is nonsingular, the projection formula in Example 2 gives \[
\begin{aligned}
\Pi(Y_1\mid\mathcal{U})
&=
E(Y_1Y_2^{\mathsf T})
\left\{
E(Y_2Y_2^{\mathsf T})
\right\}^{-1}
Y_2 \\
&=
\Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}Y_2,
\end{aligned}
\] which is equal to \(E(Y_1\mid Y_2)\) (see Section 2.3.1).
Thus, the residual is \[
Y_1-\Pi(Y_1\mid\mathcal{U})
=
Y_1-\Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}Y_2.
\] Its squared norm is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\|
Y_1-\Pi(Y_1\mid\mathcal{U})
\right\|^2
&=
\operatorname{tr}
\left(
\Sigma_{11}
-
\Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}
\right).
\end{aligned}
\]



2.4.3 Exercise 2.3

Solution. Let
\[
W
=
Z_1^2-\sigma_1^2.
\]
Then
\[
\mathcal{U}
=
\left\{
a_1W+a_2Z_2
:
a_1,a_2\in\mathbb{R}
\right\}.
\]
Because \((Z_1,Z_2)^{\mathsf T}\) is mean-zero multivariate normal, all third moments are zero. Thus,
\[
\begin{aligned}
E(Z_1W)
&=
E(Z_1^3)-\sigma_1^2E(Z_1) = 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
E(WZ_2)
&=
E(Z_1^2Z_2)-\sigma_1^2E(Z_2) = 0,
\end{aligned}
\] where we have used \[
E(Z_1^2Z_2) = E\{Z_2\underbrace{E(Z_1^2\mid Z_2)}_{\sigma_1^2 - \sigma_2^{-2}\sigma_{12}^2}\} = (\sigma_1^2 - \sigma_2^{-2}\sigma_{12}^2)E(Z_2) = 0.
\]
Thus, \(W\) is orthogonal to both \(Z_1\) and \(Z_2\). This means that the problem essentially reduces to projecting \(Z_1\) onto the linear span of \(Z_2\) alone.

The component of \(Z_1\) in the direction of \(W\) is zero. Therefore,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pi(Z_1\mid\mathcal{U})
&=
\frac{E(Z_1Z_2)}{E(Z_2^2)}Z_2 =
\sigma_{2}^{-2}\sigma_{12}Z_2.
\end{aligned}
\]

The residual is \[
Z_1-\Pi(Z_1\mid\mathcal{U})
=
Z_1-\sigma_{2}^{-2}\sigma_{12}Z_2.
\] Its variance is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{var}
\left\{
Z_1-\Pi(Z_1\mid\mathcal{U})
\right\}
&=
\sigma_1^2
-
\sigma_{2}^{-2}\sigma_{12}^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

2.5 Additional Problems

Problem 2.1
Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a closed linear subspace of \(\mathcal{H}\), and let
\[
u_0=\Pi(h\mid\mathcal{U}).
\]
Show that, for every \(u\in\mathcal{U}\),
\[
\|h-u\|^2
=
\|h-u_0\|^2
+
\|u-u_0\|^2.
\]


Problem 2.2
Let \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), and consider the Hilbert space of one-dimensional mean-zero functions of \(Z\) with finite variance. Let
\[
\mathcal{U}
=
\operatorname{span}
\left\{
Z,\,
Z^2-1
\right\}.
\]

Show that \(Z\) and \(Z^2-1\) are orthogonal.
Find \(\Pi(Z^3\mid\mathcal{U})\).
Compute the variance of

\[
Z^3-\Pi(Z^3\mid\mathcal{U}).
\]


Problem 2.3
Let \(h_1,h_2\in\mathcal{H}\). For any real number \(a\), use
\[
\|h_1-ah_2\|^2\geq 0
\]
to prove the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
\[
\left|
\langle h_1,h_2\rangle
\right|^2
\leq
\|h_1\|^2\|h_2\|^2.
\]
Show that equality holds if and only if \(h_1=ah_2\) for some scalar \(a\).


Problem 2.4
Let \(Z\) have support \(\{z_1,z_2,z_3\}\), with positive probabilities \(\pi_1,\pi_2,\pi_3\).

Find two linearly independent mean-zero functions of \(Z\) that span the space of all one-dimensional mean-zero functions of \(Z\).
What is the dimension of the space of all \(q\)-dimensional mean-zero functions of \(Z\)?

title: Preface
text:
Purpose
These notes are intended for graduate students and researchers in biostatistics and statistics who want a detailed path through semiparametric theory, influence functions, missing-data methods, and causal inference.

title: Preface
text:
Conventions

Random variables are written in uppercase and realizations in lowercase
Vectors are treated as column vectors unless stated otherwise
Expectations and inner products are taken under the true data-generating distribution unless annotated
A solution labeled “Exercise j.k” corresponds to that numbered exercise in Tsiatis (2006)

text:
Scope and attribution
This is a companion volume, not a reproduction of the source. Explanations, derivations, examples, and solutions should be written independently. Page and exercise references identify where the corresponding topic appears in the source.

title: 1  Introduction to semiparametric models
text:
1.2 Chapter Summary
A parametric model specifies the data distribution through a finite-dimensional parameter: \[
p(z; \theta), \qquad \theta \in \mathbb{R}^p.
\]
A semiparametric model retains a finite-dimensional parameter of interest, \(\beta\), while leaving other aspects of the distribution unspecified through an infinite-dimensional nuisance parameter \(\eta(\cdot)\): \[
p\{z; \beta, \eta(\cdot)\}, \qquad
\beta \in \mathbb{R}^q.
\]
The nuisance parameter is often an unknown function, such as a conditional distribution, a covariate distribution, or a baseline hazard function. But it can also be defined implicitly as the “other” aspects of the distribution that are not of direct interest. This allows the model to target \(\beta\) without imposing a full parametric constraint on the data.
Key examples include:

Restricted moment model. Only the conditional mean is specified: \[
E(Y \mid X) = \mu(X, \beta).
\]

Here \(\eta\) relates to aspects of the conditional distribution of \(Y \mid X\) other than the mean, as well as the marginal distribution of \(X\).

Proportional hazards model. Covariate effects are modeled by \(\beta\), while the baseline hazard remains unspecified: \[
\lambda(t \mid X) = \lambda_0(t)\exp(\beta^\top X).
\]

Here \(\eta = \lambda_0(t)\).

Nonparametric model. The distribution is unrestricted, and the parameter of interest is a functional of that distribution: \[
p_Z(z) = \eta(z), \qquad
\beta = E(Z) \quad \text{or} \quad E(Z^2).
\]

A semiparametric estimator \(\widehat{\beta}_n\) is typically required to be consistent and asymptotically normal: \[
\widehat{\beta}_n \xrightarrow{P} \beta,
\qquad
n^{1/2}(\widehat{\beta}_n - \beta)
\xrightarrow{D} N(0, \Sigma).
\] The significance of a semiparametric estimator is that the above holds regardless of the underlying, and potentially complex, state of \(\eta\).
The chapter motivates two key questions throughout the book:

Constructing regular semiparametric estimators;
Finding an optimal semiparametric estimator with the smallest asymptotic variance.

The answers rely on the geometry of influence functions, tangent spaces, orthogonality, and projection in Hilbert spaces.

title: 1  Introduction to semiparametric models

1.3 Additional Problems

Problem 1.1
Classify each model as parametric, semiparametric, or nonparametric. Identify the parameter of interest and any nuisance parameter.

\(Y \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), with interest in \(\mu\).
\(E(Y \mid X) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\).
\(p_Z(z)\) is unrestricted, with interest in \(E(Z)\)



Problem 1.2
Suppose that \[
E(Y \mid X) = \beta^\top X,
\] where \(X\) is a \(q\)-dimensional random vector and \(E(XX^\top)\) is nonsingular.

Show that \(\beta\) satisfies \[
E\left[X\{Y-\beta^\top X\}\right] = 0.
\]
Show that \[
\beta = \{E(XX^\top)\}^{-1}E(XY).
\]
Propose an estimator of \(\beta\) based on an iid sample \((Y_i, X_i)\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\).
Explain why this estimator does not require a parametric model for \(Y \mid X\).
